answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — an anonymous 1960s invention
answer.sourceLine: There is ‘no substantive evidence’ that Einstein ever said this. The four-year deadline first surfaced in the French beekeeping and nature press in 1965 — a decade after Einstein’s death — already pinned to his name, and the editor of The Ultimate Quotable Einstein files it under “Probably Not by Einstein.” No primary source in Einstein’s writings, speeches, or letters contains it.

source.excerpt: If the bee disappeared off the surface of the globe, man would have only four years left to live.
trail: An older idea — that over 100,000 plants depend on bees — comes from Maurice Maeterlinck’s The Life of the Bee (1901), not from Einstein.

The first link to Einstein’s name is a 1941 Canadian Bee Journal note in which beekeeper Ernest A. Fortin merely recalls ‘it was Einstein who said’ — likely confusing Darwin, Maeterlinck, and Einstein.
The apocalyptic four-year deadline appears only in French bee magazines in 1965 and The Irish Beekeeper in 1966, a decade after Einstein died.
Pollination ecologist Jeff Ollerton bluntly concludes ‘Einstein never said it’.
source.excerptNote: The French 1965 text, translated, ran: “if all bees in the world were exterminated it would take no more than four years for mankind to disappear from the globe” — already attributed to Einstein.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: Who it is pinned on
author.bio: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was the German-born theoretical physicist who developed the theory of relativity and won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics. As one of the most quoted figures of the twentieth century, his name is a magnet for feel-good and doom-laden aphorisms he never uttered. By all accounts he had no professional interest in bees or pollination ecology, and this apocalyptic bee prophecy appears nowhere in his documented work.

misattribution.heading: A textbook Einstein misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared quotes falsely credited to Einstein. Researchers agree he never said it, and no primary source connects him to the line.

items.why: Alice Calaprice, editor of The Ultimate Quotable Einstein, places the saying in her “Probably Not by Einstein” section, and Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence he ever made such a remark. The deadline version surfaces only in 1965, ten years after his death.

items.scope: The older ‘plants depend on bees’ idea
items.why: The claim that over 100,000 plant varieties rely on bees traces to Maeterlinck’s The Life of the Bee (1901) — a real source that later got tangled up with Einstein’s name.

misattribution.truthLine: The trail begins with a 1941 beekeeper vaguely recalling ‘it was Einstein who said’, and the apocalyptic four-year deadline only appears in French bee magazines in 1965–66 — its true author undocumented.

context.heading: Why the quote sticks
lead: The line fuses two things that feel authoritative: the name of the century’s most famous scientist and a specific, frightening number. Neither the number nor the name has a documented origin in Einstein’s work — but together they make an irresistible headline, and the quote has been recycled by campaigners, documentary makers, and journalists for decades.
The underlying anxiety is real — bees and other pollinators are ecologically vital — but the precise ‘four years’ countdown is folklore, not physics or entomology.
detailsBody: An older, milder idea — that over 100,000 plant species depend on bees — traces to the Belgian Nobel laureate Maurice Maeterlinck’s The Life of the Bee (1901).

In 1941 the Canadian Bee Journal printed a beekeeper, Ernest A. Fortin, vaguely recalling that ‘it was Einstein who said’ removing the bee would doom 100,000 plants — probably confusing Darwin, Maeterlinck, and Einstein.
The catastrophic ‘four years’ version appears only in 1965–66, in French nature magazines and then The Irish Beekeeper, already carrying Einstein’s name.
context.pull: Einstein never said it — and had no known interest in bees.
